rules.statement: When a token requirement selects between the user's token and the application's own client token, choose by whether a session exists, and never fall back to the client token when the user's token fails.
rules.why: A fallback would let an expired session silently call the API with the application's rights instead of the user's, and the frontend would never learn that the session had ended.
rules.check: Look for code that catches a user-token failure (refresh failed, provider unavailable) and then requests or attaches a client_credentials token.

rules.statement: In a BFF, serve the application's own client_credentials token only to a request that has a session, and answer 401 without contacting the OP when there is none.
rules.why: The session proves the caller is the BFF's own frontend. Without that check, any client on the network could call the API with the BFF's rights.
rules.check: Look for client-token paths that run before the session is resolved or checked, or that request a token from the OP when no session exists.

rules.statement: When nested operations share one lock table (for example, an outer operation holds a lock while it calls an inner service that locks the same entity), key the locks by purpose as well as by entity so the two never share a key.
rules.why: If both operations take the same key, the outer operation waits on itself until the lock times out.
rules.check: Look for a lock or semaphore keyed only by entity id where a service holding that lock calls another service that locks the same id.

rules.statement: Bound every wait on a keyed single-flight lock with a configured timeout that ends in a defined error, and make sure a cancelled holder releases its lock.
rules.why: An unbounded wait or a lock left held by a cancelled caller would block every later caller on that key.
rules.check: Look for waits on a lock or semaphore with no timeout, and for lock holders whose cancellation path doesn't release the lock in a finally or dispose.

rules.statement: Don't add a cross-replica lease or shared-state cache around acquiring a token when a second acquisition revokes nothing (client_credentials, or a token exchange whose refresh token isn't kept); a per-replica in-memory cache is enough.
rules.why: Without a reuse hazard, a lease only adds a shared-state round trip to every request, and storing the token puts a bearer credential in shared state for no gain.
rules.check: Before asking for a distributed lock or persistence around a token, check whether the grant issues a refresh token that rotation would revoke if reused. Flag code that persists such bearer tokens to shared state.

rules.statement: Don't report a singleton that holds a concurrent cache of the application's own data (such as its own client tokens) as breaking the stateless-singleton rule, as long as no request or session state goes into it and its keys come from configuration.
rules.why: The source accepts this exception explicitly: the cached data belongs to the application, not to a request, so no request's state leaks into another.
rules.check: Before reporting a stateful singleton, check whether its keys and values come only from configuration and app-owned credentials, not from request or session data.

rules.statement: Derive in-memory cache keys from registration or configuration values, never from request input, so the cache stays bounded.
rules.why: Keys taken from requests would let callers grow the cache without bound.
rules.check: Look for cache keys built from query strings, headers, route values or body fields.

rules.statement: When forwarding a browser request to an upstream API, strip the browser's Cookie, Authorization, DPoP, anti-forgery and forwarding headers, and drop the upstream's Set-Cookie headers.
rules.why: The upstream must see only the BFF, so no browser credential reaches it and the upstream can't set cookies in the browser.
rules.check: Look at proxy or forwarder transforms for request headers that are copied through, and for response Set-Cookie headers that aren't removed.

rules.statement: Before forwarding a request path that is appended to a destination base path, reject it with 400 if it contains a dot segment, an encoded '/' or '\', or a backslash.
rules.why: Such a path could leave the destination's base path once the upstream server decodes it.
rules.check: Look for code that appends a remaining request path to an upstream URI without checking for '.', '..', '%2F', '%5C' or '\'.

rules.statement: Validate a configured forwarding destination: it must be an absolute URI with no user info, query or fragment, and it must use https outside Development.
rules.why: A destination with embedded credentials, a query or plain http would leak data or weaken transport security for every forwarded request.
rules.check: Look at the options validation for destination URIs and check that the scheme, user info, query and fragment are all checked.

rules.statement: Send outbound HTTP through a named IHttpClientFactory client, not a private SocketsHttpHandler or raw HttpClient, so a host can add handlers or replace the primary handler.
rules.why: IHttpClientFactory is the framework's seam for outbound telemetry, resilience and test-server handlers. A private handler blocks all of these and forces a test to relay calls through its own listener.
rules.check: Look for `new SocketsHttpHandler`, `new HttpClient` or a custom handler-source interface in outbound code where a named client would serve.

rules.statement: Attach security-critical outbound credentials (access tokens, DPoP proofs) with a handler outside the host-configurable named-client pipeline, so handlers a host adds or a replaced primary handler can't skip it.
rules.why: Keeping the token handler outside the client means the token and its proof are attached to every request, whatever handlers a host adds.
rules.check: Look for token-attaching handlers registered with AddHttpMessageHandler on a client that hosts are told to customize.

rules.statement: Remove IHttpClientFactory's default logging handlers from a client whose request URIs may carry sensitive queries, when another component already logs those requests.
rules.why: The factory's loggers would log each forwarded URI together with its query.
rules.check: Look at named-client registrations for forwarded or proxied traffic and check whether default logging is cleared (for example with RemoveAllLoggers).

rules.statement: Don't use ':' in configuration metadata key names.
rules.why: The .NET configuration loader reads a colon as a section separator.
rules.check: Look for metadata or dictionary keys bound from configuration whose names contain ':'.

rules.statement: Validate configuration metadata at load time, and refuse dependent settings that appear without the setting that enables them, so a typo fails configuration instead of silently disabling a security behavior.
rules.why: Without this, a misspelled key would forward requests without a token rather than fail.
rules.check: Look for optional metadata or options that are read lazily with no load-time validation, or where dependent keys are accepted without their primary key.

rules.statement: Make a token or credential path fail closed: when an endpoint isn't guarded as the credential requires, throw and forward nothing, instead of forwarding without the credential.
rules.why: Forwarding without the token, or outside the cookie boundary, would silently break the security model.
rules.check: Look for code paths that skip attaching a token or continue forwarding when the endpoint's guard metadata is missing.
